Global Fuel Price Trends & Policy Impact Analysis (2020–2026)

A data-driven examination of retail fuel costs, Brent Crude pass-through, and the effectiveness of subsidies and taxation across 84 countries.

1. Global Fuel Price Overview

Between January 2020 and April 2026, the dataset captures 27,468 weekly observations across 84 countries in seven regions. All prices are normalized to USD per liter, with Brent Crude expressed in USD per barrel.

The six-year mean Brent Crude price of $106.69/bbl masks considerable volatility: a COVID-19 demand collapse drove Brent to a low of $47.97/bbl in late April 2020, while geopolitical supply fears pushed it to $130.00/bbl in late March 2022. Retail fuels tracked these swings closely in low-subsidy markets, but high-subsidy regimes severed much of the link between global benchmarks and pump prices.

2. Temporal Price Trends & Volatility

Weekly global averages reveal three distinct phases: (1) the 2020 demand shock, (2) the 2021–2022 recovery and crisis, and (3) the 2023–2026 stabilization at structurally higher levels.

In Q2 2020, Brent fell 18.9% from Q1; retail petrol, diesel, and LPG each fell ≈18.9%, indicating near-complete pass-through when policy buffers are thin. By 2022, Brent averaged $117.12/bbl (up 68.7% from 2020), lifting global mean petrol from $1.49/L to $2.51/L—again a 68.7% increase.

Volatility

2020 recorded the highest weekly volatility for both Brent (std dev = $13.53) and retail fuels. After 2023, volatility declined as prices settled into a higher plateau.

Brent-to-Retail Correlation

The overall Pearson correlation between Brent Crude and global petrol prices is 0.264, and 0.259 for diesel. These modest headline figures are driven down by the large share of high-subsidy observations where prices are administratively fixed. In low-subsidy countries, the correlation rises to 0.416; in high-subsidy countries it drops to 0.253.

3. Regional Price Disparities

Europe and Oceania consistently record the highest retail petrol prices (averages of $3.70/L and $3.66/L), reflecting high taxation and low subsidy penetration. The Middle East is the cheapest region at $1.23/L on average, driven by substantial producer subsidies.

The regional price spread—the gap between the most and least expensive regions—widened from $1.61/L in 2020 to $2.72/L in 2022, and remains above $2.75/L through 2026. This divergence is not driven by crude costs (which are global), but by divergent fiscal and subsidy regimes.

4. Impact of Subsidies and Taxation on Retail Prices

Subsidy level is the single strongest predictor of retail price levels. High-subsidy countries (including "Very High") average $0.45/L for petrol, while low-subsidy countries (including "Medium") average $2.93/L—a 84.5% price dampening effect.

During the 2022 energy crisis, low-subsidy countries saw petrol rise 7.8% from Q1 to Q2; high-subsidy countries saw a nearly identical 7.7% rise in percentage terms, but from a far lower base ($0.51/L to $0.55/L vs. $3.30/L to $3.55/L). In absolute terms, the subsidy shield is worth roughly $2.50–$3.00/L at the pump.

Subsidy Effect by Income Level

The dampening effect is strongest in high-income countries (where high-subsidy regimes are rare but extreme when present) and still substantial in low- and middle-income countries:

Taxation

Taxes represent 34.7% of the retail price in high-income countries, versus 22.9% in low-income and 21.1% in middle-income countries. High-subsidy countries collect far less fuel tax on average (15.0%) compared with low-subsidy countries (31.0%), creating a fiscal trade-off between consumer protection and public revenue.

5. Fuel Affordability by Income Level

High-income nations pay the highest absolute prices ($3.54/L petrol on average) because of steep taxation and market-based pricing. Low-income nations pay the lowest absolute prices ($1.36/L), but this is driven by subsidies rather than purchasing power. The absolute price gap between high- and low-income country averages has widened from $1.40/L in 2020 to $2.50/L in 2026.

Notably, all three income groups exhibit virtually identical coefficients of variation (CV ≈ 0.178) in their weekly price means, suggesting that macro-level price volatility is a global phenomenon. However, the welfare impact of that volatility differs sharply: a $0.50/L swing is a rounding error in high-tax Europe but a major budget shock in low-income, low-subsidy contexts.

LPG remains consistently cheaper than petrol across all income tiers, with an LPG-to-petrol price ratio of roughly 0.75–0.77, offering a modest affordability buffer where LPG infrastructure exists.

6. Key Findings & Policy Implications

  1. Subsidies are the dominant price stabilizer, but they are fiscally expensive. High-subsidy countries cut retail petrol prices by 75–90% relative to low-subsidy peers. However, these same countries collect only half the fuel-tax revenue (15% vs. 31% of retail price), limiting fiscal space for other development or climate investments.
  2. Pass-through from Brent to retail is real but highly segmented. The global Brent-petrol correlation is only 0.26 because high-subsidy observations dilute the signal. In low-subsidy, market-priced jurisdictions, the correlation jumps to 0.42 and the pass-through coefficient is 6× larger. Policymakers should monitor their own regime’s pass-through as an early-warning indicator of subsidy leakage or tax erosion.
  3. The regional price gap is widening, not closing. The spread between Europe and the Middle East grew from $1.61/L in 2020 to $2.87/L in 2026. Because crude costs are common, this divergence is entirely a function of tax and subsidy policy. Countries seeking price convergence with peers must look to fiscal levers, not commodity markets.
  4. High-income countries rely on taxation; low-income countries rely on subsidies. The result is a regressive global pattern in which the poorest nations paradoxically face lower absolute pump prices (via subsidies) but also lower public revenue to fund alternatives. A gradual shift from blanket subsidies to targeted cash transfers—combined with investment in public transit and EV infrastructure—could improve both equity and fiscal sustainability.
  5. Volatility has declined since 2022, but structural prices are permanently higher. After the 2022 spike, weekly standard deviations fell by more than half for both Brent and retail fuels. Yet annual averages remain 70% above 2020 levels. Price stabilization mechanisms (e.g., fuel price smoothing funds, strategic reserves) should be calibrated to this higher baseline, not to pre-pandemic norms.
  6. Tax and subsidy design should be region-specific. Europe and Oceania can sustain high tax rates because of high incomes and robust public transit; sudden tax cuts in these regions would erode climate goals with limited consumer relief. In contrast, Middle Eastern and African nations with large subsidy burdens should consider phased price reforms paired with social safety nets to avoid public backlash.
